Q: if (n!=0) n=0; v/s n=0; Which is more efficient and why? A:

If n is a 2's complement integral type or an unsigned integral type, then writing n = 0 directly will certainly be no slower than the version with the condition check, and a good optimising compiler will generate the same code. Some compilers compile assignment to zero as XOR'ing a register value with itself, which is a single instruction.

If n is a floating point type, a 1s' complement integral type, or a signed magnitude integral type, then the two code snippets differ in behaviour. E.g. if n is signed negative zero for example. (Acknowledge @chqrlie.) Also if n is a pointer on a system than has multiple null pointers representations, then if (n != 0) n = 0; will not assign n, when n is one of the various null pointers. n = 0; imparts a different functionality.

"will always be more efficient" is not true. Should reading n have a low cost, writing n a high cost (Think of re-writing non-volatile memory that needs to re-write a page) and is likely n == 0, then n = 0; is slower, less efficient than if (n != 0) n = 0;.

Q: Wrapped GtkLabel huge height A:

Although I'm not at all experienced with Gtk3 programming, I have seen a very similar phenomenon in Qt5.

I think what happens is that Gtk3 will set the minimum height of the label to the height it would have when wrapped to its minimum width. I mean the minimum width of the label itself, so even if the window cannot be made smaller, the label could potentially, if there were some other widgets next to it in the window.

This mechanism is described here: https://docs.gtk.org/gtk3/class.Widget.html#height-for-width-geometry-management-geometry-management

Note especially:

The minimum height for the minimum width is normally used to set the minimum size constraint on the toplevel (unless gtk_window_set_geometry_hints() is explicitly used instead).

So you could try setting a bigger minimum width constraint on the label itself, and see if that changes anything.

Q: What is the difference between client library in snowflake and Snowpark? A:

Thought of giving an comprehensive answer with execution process under the hood with my experience as I had the same doubt at the beginning. More or less this will cater the processing of snowflake queries in the infra from data engineering point of view.

Basically both approaches are using Snowflake to execute the query, but the main difference is where we are defining the logic and how that logic is translated into Snowflake SQL.

https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-connect/snowpark-connect-executing-sql

1. Python Connector + Native SQL

With Python Connector, we are basically writing the actual Snowflake SQL ourselves and sending that SQL to Snowflake.

Python Application
       │
       │  SQL Query
       ▼
Python Connector
       │
       │  Send SQL
       ▼
Snowflake
       │
       ▼
Query Optimizer
       │
       ▼
Execution Engine
       │
       ▼
Result
       │
       ▼
Python

For example:

query = """
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS bookings
FROM bookings
WHERE booking_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
"""

cursor.execute(query)
result = cursor.fetchall()

Here, we are telling Snowflake directly:

"This is the SQL I want you to execute."

So Snowflake receives almost exactly what we wrote and then its optimizer decides how to execute it.

The important thing here is that Python is mainly acting as the client.

Python creates the SQL → Connector sends it → Snowflake executes it → Result comes back to Python.

2. Snowpark DataFrame

With Snowpark, instead of writing the SQL directly, we define the transformation using Python DataFrame APIs.

Whole guide is here : https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/data-engineering-pipelines-with-snowpark-python/

For example:

df = session.table("BOOKINGS")

result = (
    df
    .filter(col("BOOKING_DATE") >= "2026-01-01")
    .group_by("CUSTOMER_ID")
    .agg(count("*").alias("BOOKINGS"))
)

Here we are not actually executing Python operations on the data.

This is the important part.

Python Code
     │
     │  Snowpark DataFrame API
     ▼
Snowpark
     │
     │  Builds logical query
     ▼
Snowflake SQL
     │
     ▼
Query Optimizer
     │
     ▼
Snowflake Execution Engine
     │
     ▼
Result

So Snowpark is basically giving us a Python interface to construct operations that will eventually execute inside Snowflake.

3. So what is actually happening?

This is where I think the confusion usually happens.

People sometimes think:

Snowpark DataFrame

Python
  ↓
DataFrame loaded into Python
  ↓
Python filters data
  ↓
Python performs aggregation

But that's not what normally happens.

It is more like:

Python

df.filter(...)
df.group_by(...)
df.agg(...)
        │
        ▼
Snowpark builds the query plan
        │
        ▼
Snowflake
        │
        ▼
SQL execution
        │
        ▼
Data stays inside Snowflake

So if we have 1 TB of data in Snowflake, Snowpark is not downloading that 1 TB into Python just because we created a DataFrame.

The computation is pushed to Snowflake.

4. Native SQL vs Snowpark

Let's say we want to do this:

SELECT
    customer_id,
    AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue
FROM bookings
WHERE country = 'UAE'
GROUP BY customer_id

Using Python Connector:

cursor.execute("""
SELECT
    customer_id,
    AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue
FROM bookings
WHERE country = 'UAE'
GROUP BY customer_id
""")

We manually write the SQL.

Using Snowpark:

df = session.table("BOOKINGS")

result = (
    df
    .filter(col("COUNTRY") == "UAE")
    .group_by("CUSTOMER_ID")
    .agg(
        avg("REVENUE").alias("AVG_REVENUE")
    )
)

Conceptually both are trying to produce the same thing.

             Same Data
                 │
        ┌────────┴────────┐
        │                 │
   Native SQL          Snowpark
        │                 │
        ▼                 ▼
   SQL Query        DataFrame API
        │                 │
        │          Query Construction
        │                 │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 ▼
          Snowflake Optimizer
                 │
                 ▼
        Snowflake Execution

So the biggest difference is how we express the computation, not necessarily where the computation happens.

5. The biggest difference

With native SQL, we have more direct control.

Python
   │
   ▼
SQL
   │
   ▼
Snowflake

We decide exactly what SQL gets executed.

With Snowpark:

Python
   │
   ▼
Snowpark DataFrame API
   │
   ▼
Logical Plan
   │
   ▼
Snowflake SQL / Execution Plan
   │
   ▼
Snowflake

Snowpark gives us an abstraction layer(wrapper???).

6.Performance & Cost(Most Crucial in data intensive apps)

Snowpark and Native SQL can be almost the same in performance if they result in the same Snowflake execution plan. The real performance difference is usually:

                    Performance
                         │
        ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
        │                                 │
   Native SQL                         Snowpark
        │                                 │
        ▼                                 ▼
SQL directly                    DataFrame operations
        │                                 │
        └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                       ▼
                Snowflake Optimizer
                       │
                       ▼
                Query Execution
                       │
                       ▼
                  Warehouse

So Snowpark is not inherently slower just because you're using Python.

Hope this gives you an 360 degree view of the two approaches.

Q: How can I prevent duplicate JSON-LD schema output in WordPress? A:

When dealing with duplicate JSON-LD in WordPress, focus on schema reconciliation rather than outright prevention. Here's a technical approach:

1. **Audit Existing Schema**

  • Use Chrome DevTools (Elements > Search for 'application/ld+json') to identify all JSON-LD blocks

  • Note all `@type` declarations and property conflicts

2. **Filter-Based Reconciliation**

For Rank Math specifically:

```php

add_filter('rank_math/json_ld', function($data) {

   // Target only business-related schemas

   foreach ($data as $key =\> $entity) {

       if (isset($entity\['@type'\]) && 

           ($entity\['@type'\] === 'LocalBusiness' || 

            $entity\['@type'\] === 'Organization')) {

           // Merge your custom properties here

           $data\[$key\]\['hasOfferCatalog'\] = \[/\* your offer data \*/\];

       }

   }

   return $data;

}, 20); // Higher priority than default

```

3. **@id Reconciliation**

When separate blocks are unavoidable:

  • Establish canonical `@id` references (e.g., `#primary-business`)

  • Use `sameAs` for duplicate properties

  • Maintain consistent `url` and `name` properties

4. **Validation Tools**

  • Test merged output with [Google's Rich Results Test](https://search.google.com/test/rich-results)

  • Check for warnings about conflicting properties

**Key Technical Consideration**: WordPress plugins often store schema data in transients. Clear these (`wp_cache_flush()`) after making changes to see immediate results.

**Actionable Takeaway**: Today, run a schema audit using DevTools and note any property conflicts between your custom schema and Rank Math's output - focus first on `address`, `telephone`, and `priceRange` inconsistencies.

Q: Combine two columns and add into one new column A:

Generally, I agree with @kgrittn's advice. Go for it.

But to address your basic question about concat(): it is useful if you need to deal with null values - and null has neither been ruled out in your question nor in the one you refer to.

If you can rule out null values, the good old (SQL standard) concatenation operator || is still the best choice, and @luis' answer is just fine:

SELECT col_a || col_b;

If either of your columns can be null, the result would be null in that case. You could defend with COALESCE:

SELECT COALESCE(col_a, '') || COALESCE(col_b, '');

But that gets tedious quickly with more arguments. That's where concat() comes in, which never returns null, not even if all arguments are null. The manual:

NULL arguments are ignored.

SELECT concat(col_a, col_b);

The remaining corner case for both alternatives is where all input columns are null in which case we still get an empty string ''. To get null instead:

SELECT CASE
          WHEN col_a IS NULL THEN col_b
          WHEN col_b IS NULL THEN col_a
          ELSE col_a || col_b
       END;

This gets more complex with more columns quickly. Again, use concat(), but add a check for the special condition:

SELECT CASE WHEN (col_a, col_b) IS NULL THEN NULL
            ELSE concat(col_a, col_b) END;

How does this work?
(col_a, col_b) is shorthand for ROW (col_a, col_b). And a row type is only null if all columns are null. Detailed explanation:

  • NOT NULL constraint over a set of columns

Also, use concat_ws() to add separators between elements (ws for "with separator").

An expression like the one in Kevin's answer:

SELECT $1.zipcode || ' - ' || $1.city || ', ' || $1.state;

is tedious to prepare for null values in PostgreSQL 8.3 (without concat()). One way (of many):

SELECT COALESCE(
         CASE
            WHEN $1.zipcode IS NULL THEN $1.city
            WHEN $1.city    IS NULL THEN $1.zipcode
            ELSE $1.zipcode || ' - ' || $1.city
         END, '')
       || COALESCE(', ' || $1.state, '');

Function volatility is only STABLE

concat() and concat_ws() are STABLE functions, not IMMUTABLE because they can invoke datatype output functions (like timestamptz_out) that depend on locale settings.
Explanation by Tom Lane.

This prohibits their direct use in index expressions. If you know that the result is actually immutable in your case, you can work around this with an IMMUTABLE function wrapper. Examples:

  • Create an immutable clone of concat_ws
  • Does PostgreSQL support "accent insensitive" collations?
